Bill No. 19 to consolidate and amend the Railway Act.-Hon. J. D. Reid.

On motion of Hon. Mr. Ballantyne Bill No. 122 to amend the Canada Shipping Act (Pilotage and Harbour Masters) was read the second time and the House went into Committee on the Bill, Mr. J. M. Douglas in the Chair.
On section 1-Minister may be appointed pilotage authority by Governor in Council:

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
When the resolution was before the Committee some days ago I explained the object of this Bill. First, it is to enable the Governor in Council to take over the pilotage system in accordance with the recommendation made by

the Royal Commission' appointed about a year ago. I refer to the ports of Halifax, Sydney, St. John, N.B., Victoria, Vancouver and Nanaimo. The object of the introduction of this Bill is to very' much increase the efficiency of the pilotage system, something that is greatly needed at the present time. Secondly, it is to' increase the dues on ships of over 1,000 registered tons from $5 to $7, in order that the harbour masters in certain ports instead of only being able to draw a maximum of $600 a year, providing that the fees reach that amount, will be enabled to draw $1,200, provided the fees reach that amount.
Is that not the same Bill that came up the other day?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, this is a different Bill.
Is there a modification?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Bill that the
hon. member refers to dealt with the ease of the harbour masters at the port of Halifax. This applies to the harbour masters of other ports.
Do I understand the minister to say that this clause, 432, will authorize the minister to supersede the pilotage corporations in various districts?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No, it does not do that. The pilotage systems of Quebec and Montreal have been under the Minister of Marine and Fisheries for twelve or thirteen years. It in- no way interferes with the local pilotage authorities. It simply takes jurisdiction out of the local pilotage commissions at the ports I name and vests that authority in the Governor in Council, or with reference to these ports, in the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, -the same- as it is in regard to the ports of Quebec and Montreal.
On section 3-Harbour masters' salaries increased from $600 to $1,200:
In the harbour of Sydney there are no dues or charges against ships coming in. Does this Act provide for a new schedule of charges against ships coming into that port?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
At North Sydney the dues levied against ships in the year 1918 amounted to $839.50. The harbour-master

there draws a remuneration of $600. If the dues on ships amount to $1,000 his salary will .be $1,000, but in any event it will not exceed the maximum amount of $1,200. The object of this Bill is to increase the tonnage dues on ships over 1,000 tons from $5 to $7 in order that these underpaid harbour-masters may draw a maximum salary of $1,200 each providing the dues reach that amount.
Has the minister appointed a harbour-master at the port of Canso yet?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am sorry I cannot answer the hon. gentleman now, but I shall inquire. I noticed his question on tire Order Paper and I hope to be able to give him the information in the course of a day or so.

The harbour-master at Canso died some months ago, and I was informed that the Civil Service Commission was to make the appointment. I have not heard that an appointment has been made. I would like to know if the appointment has been made and who the officer is.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I will be very glad to look into that and let the hon. member know at the earliest possible moment. Unfortunately, I was ill for four months, and I was not able to keep up to date with all these things that transpired during my absence.
On the preamble:
Might I ask the minister what he understands by the provision that he shall supersede the existing pilotage authority?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Outside of the ports of Montreal and Quebec they have local pilotage commissions and they give their services voluntarily. The object of this Bill is to do away with the local pilotage commissions, and to invest the Minister of Marine with the same authority that he now enjoys as regards the ports of Quebec and Montreal-we want to put all the ports of Canada on the same footing.

Is there any general provision under this Act for the pensioning of pilots? I understand that in the case of the river St. Lawrence pilots there is an arrangement under which a retiring pilot

receives a pension. The minister will find, after administering the pilotage branch of his department for a short time, that there will be a great deal of dissatisfaction unless a uniform system of pensions for pilots is adopted. Is there any provision whereby the same practice which prevails in regard to the St. Lawrence pilots will be applied to the pilots of Halifax, Sydney, and other ports, which the minister is bringing under the control of 'the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. gentleman's point is very well taken. Unless we have uniformity as regards pensions there certainly will not be satisfaction in the ease of 'the pilotage systems throughout Canada that are now coming under the control of the Minister of Marine. The only pilots that receive a pension at the present time are those in the Quebec district. In 1906, when the Hon. Mr. Brodeur was Minister of Marine, there were one hundred and sixteen pilots in that district, which was deemed too many, and in order to reduce the number to seventy-five-there are only sixty-one at present-it was agreed by Order in Council at that time that when a Quebec pilot reached the age of sixty-five he should be retired on a pension of $300. The amount required for paying the Quebec pensions has to be voted by Parliament each year, but the hon. gentleman is quite right in his statement that the pension should not he restricted to Quebec pilots. Therefore I hope, providing it meets with the approval of the Government, to introduce legislation at the next session of Parliament, to either discontinue the pensions to the Quebec pilots, or to grant a reasonable pension to 'the pilots generally. I am very much in favour of the latter course, because the pilotage examination is now very strict. I have in mind one pilot in the Quebec district, a young man of only thirty-eight years of age, who was not able to pass the eyesight test this year. When pilots have to go through a long apprenticeship and serve a number oif years as branch pilots, and then fail to pass the necessary examination, which is a strict one and takes place annually, there should be some provision made for them in the way of a pension.

I understand the earnings of the Quebec pilots are pooled, and the amount divided at the end of the year, each pilot receiving the same sum. Am I correct in that? If so, what were
the average earnings of those pilots last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
All the pilots in
the Queibec district do not receive the pension of $300 annually voted by Parliament, but only those who were in the service at the time the Order in Council referred to was passed. When those pilots reach the age of sixty-five they are retired on a pension of $300-the pilots that entered the service subsequent to the passing of that Order in Council do not receive a pension from Parliament, but draw a pension from the pilotage pension fund, to which the hon. gentleman has just referred. The gross earnings of the Quebec pilotage district amounted last year to $125,000.

How much did
that yield to each pilot?
Mr. BALLAN'TYNE:	I understand the
pilots have a very large fund amounting to something like $90,000, and they give each pilot $300 a year, but the fund is administered by the pilots themselves.

The minister
does not mean that the total earnings of a pilot for a year would only amount to $300?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
1 want to ascertain how much each pilot earned during the year out of the business?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That would depend a great deal upon the number of trips that each pilot would make. Some pilots earn $1,200 a year, the maximum earnings being about $1,800. The steamship companies sometimes prefer to hate a certain pilot always pilot their boats, and therefore some favoured pilots make more money than others.

I am not certain that I correctly apprehend the situation with respect to pensions from the statement of the minister. I understood from the discussion which took place the other evening, that pensions were paid to retired pilots, but were not paid to pilots in active service. Am I correct in that understanding? I can see no ground why a pilot earning from $1,200 to $1,800 should get any pension from the Government, but there is very good reason for pensioning a pilot who has spent his life in the service and be-

comes incapacitated for duty if there is a pension system for that purpose. Do I understand that the active pilots who earn a certain amount each year also receive a pension?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Two systems of pensions apply to the Quebec pilots. Under the one, pilots that were in the service in 1906 are retired when they reach the age of sixty-five and are given a pension of 1300, which is annually voted by Parliament. Under the other system, pilots that might not possibly pass the pilotage examination, from poor eyesight or other causes, receive a pension from the Pilots' Pension Fund.
Then some pilots that were in the sendee in 1906, and are still pursuing their calling and earning a certain amount every year, also receive a pension?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They will not receive a pension while they are in the service, but when they attain the age of sixty-five years they will be retired on a pension of $300 a year. The Order in Council passed in 1906 is very specific in its terms that the pilots referred to are to receive such pension, and I felt that we could not ignore its provisions. However, at the next session of Parliament I think it would be well to adopt a pension system, as the leader of the Opposition has suggested, applicable to all the pilots throughout Canada, and not merely to those in the Quebec district.
Does the Government provide boats for the pilots?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
What does that cost the country ?#

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That would depend upon the port to which the hon. gentleman has reference. I have not got the details of the information here, but the department does provide pilot boat at all the leading ports.

I understand that the pilots of Halifax, St. John and other ports along the Atlantic coast, supply their own boats. When they go out to meet steamships they do so in their own boats and pay the expenses of those boats. In the case of the St. Lawrence pilots, however, it seems that the Government furnishes them with boats. My question is:
* Mr. Sinclair.]
How many boats is the Government operating at Quebec or Rimouski, and what is the annual cost of maintenance?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have only one steamer. I am sorry I did not anticipate that question being asked. I will certainly try to get the information for the hon. member. In as far as the ports of Halifax and St. John are concerned, they did provide their own boats, and if we took over those pilotage systems I think it would be only right that we should provide boats for the pilots. All the pilots ought to be treated in the same way.

For the information
of the hon. member for Guysborough, I may say that the only boat furnished by the Government is at Father Point. At the time the Government made the change from Bic to Father Point the pilots had their own schooner to go from the wharf to the steamers coming up there. The change involved an added distance of 18 miles, and it was understood then that the department would supply the pilots with a boat. They have only one boat at Father Point to take the pilots from the wharf to the steamers and from the steamers to the wharf.

The pilots of the harbour of Sydney have an Act of incorporation and have been conducting their business entirely under their own control. They have officials of the organization and also of the pilotage commission. -The dues are collected, I think, at the customs house at North Sydney and Sydney and then passed over to the secretary of the association, who divides the money among the pilots. Now I understand some new machinery will be created by which the pilotage business will be conducted under the control of the department. I mentioned to the minister the other day that there are some officials connected with that work who will likely be put out of office altogether, and I would like to know if he has anything in contemplation as to what he is going to do with them. It is pretty hard lines to deprive men altogether of their means of livelihood. The secretary of the pilotage commission and the chairman are on salary, and also the secretary-treasurer of the association.
I think it is rather the custom of the Government, when a radical change of this kind takes place, to look after, in some degree at all events, the old officials,

as no doubt the changes are made in the general advantage of the country. It was no doubt for that reason that the pension system was adopted by the department in 1906 in connection with the change made in the St. Lawrence pilotage system. Now that this change is taking place I would like to know if the minister has any well defined policy as to what he is going to substitute for the machinery that is now looking after the pilotage systems in such places as St. John, Halifax and Sydney Harbour, and also on the Pacific coast, where there must be some pilotage companies of the same class and character.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is not our intention to interfere with any of the permanent officials. There is at Sydney a secretary by the name of Mr. Kimber, and it is not our intention, so far as I know, to replace him. Of course the local pilotage commissions will disappear. I understand there are four pilotage commissioners there drawing a very small remuneration, but as a rule these commissioners give their services gratuitously. That will be the only change, with the exception that we will appoint a local superintendent of pilots there who has had seafaring experience and holds a master mariner's certificate. In all other respects the pilotage system will remain the same, except that the regulations will be carried out a little more strictly, and, I hope, a little more efficiently.

Has the minister determined what kind of a man he wants as superintendent of pilots? I notice that there is an age limit as to the pilots themselves. Has the minister 5 p.m. thought of any age limit or any particular qualifications for the superintendent that he proposes to appoint?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have not set any particular age, but I would like to get a man somewhere around forty or forty-five, or in any event not older than fifty,-a seafaring man who holds a master mariner's certificate and thoroughly understands navigation, in order that he can keep the pilotage system under his charge in the highest possible state of efficiency. We have not definitely fixed what his remuneration will be, but we hope to make it fair and reasonable. Such appointments would have to be made by the Civil Service Commission on the recommendation of the Department of Marine.

I understand the minister to say that there is to be no change of official's that are really necessary for the carrying on of the work now. At the present time there are two men in connection with the pilotage commission in Sydney, a treasurer and paymaster and a secretary. The latter is Mr. Kimiber; I forget the name of the paymaster. I understand that those officials are to be continued, and that the same system of collecting dues from the ships will obtain just as it does now.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I will -qualify my
answer by stating that it is not our intention to disturb the local conditions at all. The dues will be levied and collected in the usual way, and we hope to retain all of the officials there. But if the local superintendent should report to the department that it will not be necessary to have a secretary and also a treasurer-I do not know that he will so report-some action might have to be taken. It is hard to anticipate what recommendations will be made; but generally speaking it is not my intention or that of the department to interfere in any way with those old efficient officials.

Under present conditions the pilotage commissioners meet twice a year to receive applications for the positions of pilots and pilot apprentices. If a pilot dies or gets too old, some one must be appointed to take his place. How is that class of work to be carried on now, and how are apprentices to be obtained and appointed? How are pilots to be appointed, say, in Sydney harbour?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If a vacancy occurred in the pilotage system at Sydney or if apprentice pilots were required, the local superintendent of pilots would make the necessary recommendation to the general superintendent of pilots whom I hope to have at Ottawa in charge of all local superintendents. In that way we get the necessary information. We are guided very largely by the advice of the local pilotage man and of the general superintendent of pilots here.

The shipping at Sydney Harbour is very large indeed; it must rank third among the shipping lists of Canada. The maintaining of the pilotage system there at a first-class standard is very important to shipowners and to the good name

of the port. I fear that the minister will find it difficult to maintain an efficient system by depending entirely upon some one individual who has exclusive jurisdiction in the selection of apprentices and pilots. I understood the minister to say the other day that some form of examination would be prescribed for these pilots. Will this examination be held at local points? It would be inconvenient for men at St. John, Halifax or Sydney to be obliged to go to Ottawa for examination. Moreover, persons concerned in these examinations would like to know as soon as possible what kind of examination they will have to pass.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Quebec district has 62 pilots and 10 apprentice pilots; the Montreal district has 51 pilots; Sydney has 33 pilots and 7 apprentice pilots. We have found the system under the Minister of Marine and a competent local superintendent to work admirably in the Montreal and Quebec districts. The examinations would, of course, be held locally. Here is just a line or two from the recommendations of the Royal Commission which was appointed to inquire into the conditions in these pilotage districts:
That the tests far the eyesight and hearing of the pilots, and (present apprentices, be conducted on a standard basis, the same system applying in the various districts.
The basis for examination will be the same in all the ports. They go on to say:
That such tests should be held annually in the cases of pilots and apprentices under the age of 65, and semi-annually in the case of pilots between the ag>s of 65 and 70.
They further recommend that pilots and apprentice pilots undergo each year an examination as regards eyesight, colourblindness and hearing, before a medical officer and an officer of the Department of Marine, both selected by the minister; and that sight tests shall be the same as those passed by candidates for masters' and mates' examinations. I assure hon. members that my only object in asking the Committee to pass this Bill is that of improving the standard of the pilotage system of Canada. The shipping people are asking for this legislation; the Royal Commission strongly recommends it. Our experience in Montreal and Quebec districts has been so eminently satisfactory that I have no hesitation in recommending the adoption of the Bill.

Preamble agreed to.

Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

maintopic: RED CROSS SOCIETY INCORPORATION ACT AMENDMENT.

speechtext:
On motion of Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden (Prime (Minister), Bill No. 130, to amend an Act to incorporate The Canadian Red Cross (Society, was read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. J. M. Douglas in the Chair.
On section 1-Purposes of the society extended to include work in times of peace.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: RED CROSS SOCIETY INCORPORATION ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The section which is proposed to be amended, section 2 of chapter 68 of the statutes of 1909, reads as follows:-
The purposes of the society shall be,-
1.	To furnish volunteer aid to the sick and wounded of armies in time of war, in accordance with the spirit and conditions of the conference of Geneva of October, 1863, and also of the treaty of the Red Cross or the treaty of Geneva of August twenty-second, 1864, to which Great Britain has given its adhesion ;
2.	To perform all the duties devolved upon a national society by each nation which has acceded to said treaty, but in affiliation with the said British Red Cross Society;
3.	To euoceed to and take over al the rights and property heretofore or now held and enjoyed by, and all the duties heretofore performed by, the unincorporated association known as the Canadian Red Cross Society.
It is proposed by this Bill to add to that section as subsection 4, the following:-
"(4) In time of peace to carry on and assist in work for the Improvement of health, the prevention of disease and the mitigation of suffering throughout the wcrld."
When the Bill was introduced, I explained that 'there had been held at Geneva a convention at which a number of the Red Cross societies of the world were represented, and at which a conclusion was reached that the Red Cross societies should undertake work of this kind in time of peace. The idea impressed itself very much upon the representatives of the different nations assembled at the Peace Conference at Paris, and when (the Covenant of the League of Nations was finally presented and accepted, it included this clause:
The members of the League agree to encourage and promote the establishment and co-operation -of duly authorized voluntary national Red Cross organizations having as purposes the improvement of health, the prevention of disease and the mitigation of suffering throughout the world.
President Wilson when he presented the final draft of the League of Nations' Coven-

ant at a.plenary session of the Peace Conference held on the 28th April, last, spoke of this article as follows:
Article XXV specifically mentions the Ked Cross as one of the international organizations which are to connect and work with the work of the League.
The purpose of this Bill is merely to empower the Canadian Red Cross Society, in connection with other societies of a similar character throughout the world, to continue to carry on its work in time of peace as well as in time of war.

maintopic: RED CROSS SOCIETY INCORPORATION ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Representatives of the Red Cross organization, the St. John Ambulance Association, the St. John Ambulance Brigade and the Victorian Order of Nurses met in Ottawa about two or three months ago with the idea and for the purpose of uniting these four organizations into one organization for work in Canada. At that meeting it was generally understood that an amalgamation of these four organizations would take place. Later on something happened whereby the Red Cross Society changed iits attitude towards the suggested movement. I might say, in explanation, that the Red Cross Society has up to this time been an organization which functions only during times of war. The St. John Ambulance Association has been functioning during times of peace and carrying on a rather extensive teaching programme which has resulted in turning out first aid assistants to physicians and others in need of that kind of work. The St. John Ambulance Brigade is ian organization which employed these trained students and administered 'that particular part of the work. The Victorian Order of Nurses, as every hon. member knows, is a nurses' organization, the ramifications of which pretty well cover Canada. It seemed to the representatives of these four organizations that, to prevent over-lapping and also to prevent these different organizations from so-to-speak, ploughing the same field for funds to carry on their work, it would be a good thing to combine them. I was, therefore, somewhat surprised the other day to find the Prime Minister bringing in this amendment to the Act to incorporate the Canadian Red Cross Society. I am not yet quite sure as to why the Red Cross Society, a war organization, is now desirous of carrying on the same work in times of peace, in view of the fact that there are in this country other organizations already organized for that work,
including a teaching staff to turn out these voluntary aid nurses, an organization to administer them and the Victorian Order of Nurses as well. I am not particularly criticising this amendment; I am speaking rather with the idea of getting a little more information upon the policy of the Red Cross Society now since it intends entering an entirely new field, that is to say, to function during times.of peace.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: RED CROSS SOCIETY INCORPORATION ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I do not know that I can give my hon. friend very much more information than I have given already. I did not know anything about the meeting to which he alludes, and I think it would be most desirable that there should be a working arrangement between the organizations in question. But I should like to point out to him that there cannot be this working arrangement until this society receives the power which it is asking for now, and I should not imagine there would be any possible objection to giving to a society which has done such wonderful work in every country throughout the world during the war an opportunity of continuing and extending its usefulness during times of peace. It is to be hoped that those who are entrusted with the management of the different organizations in question will not be led astray by any feeling of jealously or rivalry, but that they will unite in a common and concerted action and co-operation for the purpose of doing the most good that they can. But it is quite impossible for this society to engage in any work of. the kind until it receives the power which by this amendment it is proposed to give it.

maintopic: RED CROSS SOCIETY INCORPORATION ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I am very much pleased to hear the words of the Prime Minister, because they are words with which I thoroughly agree. I was present at the meeting referred to by the hon. member (Mr. A. Thompson), and I know the attitude that was taken there. The purpose was not to amalgamate all these organizations; the purpose was to have a working arrangement between them. It would be most undesirable at the present time to have two or more large bodies, well recognized and all holding good positions in the life of our people, engaged in similar work. We want to prevent everything in the shape of overlapping, so that the interest of the people will be best served at the least possible cost. For that reason we are desirous of having a working arrangement between all these organizations, and I hope the Prime

Minister will render all assistance possible in seeing that that arrangement is brought about.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: RED CROSS SOCIETY INCORPORATION ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I certainly shall use all my influence towards that end, because I entirely agree with what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cowan) has said. In speaking of the excellent service that has beerT given by the Red Cross, I hope I shall not be. understood as lacking in appreciation of the splendid work done by all the other organizations which have been spoken of this afternoon.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

RESOLUTION TO PROVIDE ?10,000,000 FOR THE PROVINCES IN AID OF TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
On motion of Hon. J. A. Calder (Min ister of Immigration) the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. J. M. Douglas (Strath-cona) in the Chair:
1.	To bring in a measure for the promotion of Technical Education in Canada.
2.	That for the purpose of promoting and
assisting technical education in Canada, the following sums, aggregating ten million dollars, shall be appropriated and made available for payment out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada, during each fiscal year for the period of ten years beginning with the year ending the thirty-first day of March, one thousand nine hundred	and twenty,	namely	:

Probably a brief general
statement from me at the present time will expedite the work of the Committee before we get down to consideration of the clauses

in detail. It will not be necessary for me at this stage to make any extended remarks with reference to the desirability of providing for technical education throughout Canada. That is a matter that has been discussed in the House time and again in the course of the past ten years, and as I understand the situation, there has practically been unanimity in the view that some action in this regard should be taken. If I mistake not, the last time the subject was before the House was in 1915, on a motion introduced by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), and there was at that time a very full discussion of the whole subject. At the conclusion of the debate the Hon. Mr. Rogers, then Minister of Public Works, intimated to the House that it might be expected that the Federal Government would at an early session bring down a measure providing for federal assistance to the cause of technical education.
The resolution before the Committee sets forth the conditions under which the Federal Government now purposes to give assistance to the provinces in the carrying on of technical education work. It will be remembered that in 1910 a Royal Commission was appointed to investigate this whole subject. The commission consisted of seven members, with Dr. James Robertson as chairman. The commissioners were gentlemen eminently qualified to carry on that investigation, and a very large number of meetings were held throughout Canada in about a hundred different places. Considerable evidence was taken, some 1,400 or 1,500 witnesses having been called.
The whole situation in Canada was very carefully and exhaustively reviewed, and in addition to their work in the Dominion the commission went abroad, conducting investigations in England, Scotland, Ireland, France, Germany, Switzerland, and the United States, with a view to ascertaining what these countries had done in the way of providing for vocational and technical education. As a result of all these inquiries held in Canada and abroad, the commission prepared an exhaustive and elaborate report, which was submitted to Parliament in 1913. Any member of the Committee who desires to make himself thoroughly acquainted with conditions that existed at that time in Canada and in the foreign countries which the commission visited will find that report a veritable storehouse of useful and interesting information. Indeed, the report of that commission is regarded as one of the best treatises that can be
found anywhere on the subject of technical education, and any member interested in the questions involved in the subject will find a perusal of the report profitable. The report recommended that the Parliament of Canada should set aside annually a sum of $3,350,000 for a period of ten years to assist the provinces in carrying on vocational work and technical education. The Government has not seen its way clear to adopt the recommendations of the commissioners in that respect. The investigations and report were made prior to the war, the report having been submitted in 1913, and every member of the Committee will realize that conditions in Canada to-day are not what they were in 1913.
The statement made to-day by the hon. Minister of Finance clearly indicates the obligations that have been cast upon the Dominion Government as a result of the war. I have no hesitation in saying that in my judgment the provinces are at present in equally as good a financial position as the Dominion, if not better, and consequently there is not the necessity now for rendering assistance to the provinces to the same extent as there was in 1913 or prior to that date. At any rate, the Government, after a careful consideration of the entire situation, has come to the conclusion that for the present at least we should not attempt to provide the amount of federal assistance that was suggested by the commission. The purpose of this resolution is to provide for this work, covering a period of ten years, grants aggregating $10,000,000 for distribution among the provinces, the grants to begin this year at $700,000 and to be increased annually by $100,000, until a maximum total appropriation of $1,100,000 is made available; and that to continue until the end of the ten-year period. In adopting this scale we have followed the plan that was adopted in the case of grants under the Agricultural Aids Act passed by parliament some years ago. In other words, the grants under the proposed Bill for technical education will be on all fours with those that are payable under the Agricultural Aids Act, and the distribution in the main is along practically the same lines, although there is a slight variation which I do not think is necessary in this case. I think probably it -might save time if I should leave the details of the scheme for -consideration when we come to each clause.
Broadly speaking, it is proposed that we should, by agreement with the provinces, undertake to expend for technical educa-
.3166

tion purposes a sum beginning with $700,000 to be increased gradually up to $1,100,000, the whole to be spread over a period of ten years, and the total amount expended at the end of that time to be $10,000,000. Last year this subject was brought up at the Provincial Conference held in Ottawa,-the largest conference, I think, that has ever been held here. The subject was very fully discussed and at the conclusion there was practically a unanimity of opinion that there would be no difficulty in carrying out a plan of this kind. In previous debates in this House a good deal of attention was given to the question of jurisdiction. In the debate which occured in 1916 on the motion of the hon. member for Maisonneuve, probably the greater portion of the discussion centered around this question, and while that point may be to a certain extent at issue, we were assured at the conference held last fall by all the provinces that they did not anticipate any serious difficulty in this direction. It was rightly pointed out that under the Agricultural Aids Act they have experienced very little if any difficulty. The Minister of Agriculture here, and the Ministers of Agriculture in the provincial Governments, have readily been able to arrive at an agreement whereby the moneys provided by that Act should be expended.
All the provincial prime ministers who were present at the conference held last fall assured the Federal Government that they did not anticipate the slightest difficulty in that regard. They also assured us that, to make certain that these moneys were properly and legitimately expended they would not put any difficulty in the way of the Federal Government going into these institutions and seeing that the money was expended for the purpose for which it had been provided. If the measure is approved by the Committee and the House I think we may anticipate no trouble in that connection.
It seems to me that it is not necessary at this time to say anything as to the advisability of having work of this kind done. While many of our provinces have established technical educational institutions, while they are carrying on vocational training in its various branches, and while many are conducting industrial night schools, I think we will all agree that the amount of work of that kind which is being done in Canada is not as extensive as it should be. There is an actual need for an advance in this respect. We all know what the condition is throughout the world. There is go-
[Mr. CaWer.I
ing to be keen competition in the industrial field and, if Canada is going to play her part in the struggle that we must expect for some years to come, it seems to me that it is absolutely necessary that we should take a forward step in the direction of fitting the workmen engaged in our industries, and also in training the youth of the land, so that we may become supreme in our various industries. Work has been done in this direction in most of. the provinces and every credit must be given for what has been accomplished in that direction. We have some splendid technical institutions in Canada now. The number is not as large as it should be. These institutions are very costly as regards capital expenditure and maintenance. I think all will agree with me that everything that can be done by the Federal Government in rendering assistance in order that this work may be extended throughout Canada will be very generously approved not only by Parliament, but by the people of Canada as well.

Mr. Chairman, I am
sure that we entirely agree with the minister in the statement that he has made that no argumentative persuasion is necessary to convince this Committee that technical education is a prime necessity in this country. That is one of the subjects upon which we are all agreed. It was in 1910 that the commission, with Dr. Robertson at its head, was appointed in connection with technical education. I had the pleasure of attending some of the sittings in different parts of the country, and I was pleased to see that they were going so thoroughly into the subject. Although I never had the opportunity of reading their report, I believe it is a first-class accumulation of useful information and direction along the lines for which the commission was appointed. I also agree with the minister that at this stage in the life of Canada, when it is so absolutely necessary that we should take a first position in all productive efforts, it is essential that our manufactures should be of the first order and that everything that is turned out in competition with keen producers in other parts of the world should be of the finest quality and the best workmanship. When we consider all these things it is to be understood at once how necessary it is for us that our workmen and women should have the proper training and education to compete with producers all over the world.
We have in Nova Scotia a very excellent technical college. That college was estab-

lished at a great deal of expense, possibly an amount of money that might be regarded as a little beyond the capacity of the province at the time. Nevertheless, the people have approved of the expenditure and many of our young people have received more benefit from it perhaps than from the expenditure on any other educational institution in the province. There is a working arrangement between the different universities and the college by which two years of training in any one of the universities counts for attendance at college, and in two years more students can get their degrees in the particular lines in which they seek to graduate, such as engineering or whatever else they might set out to study. It is well to make this technical education as practical, and to bring it as close to the people, as possible. In Nova Scotia we get the benefit of the larger training and the wider knowledge that is acquired at that college through several smaller schools all over the province principally in connection with our coal mines.	We have small
branches established here and there in which classes are trained so as to enable them to pass for the different grades of officers in connection with the coal mines. They take the courses for underground manager, manager, and other positions, all of which call for an examination, and candidates have succeeded in passing most creditable examinations by attending these schools, which are usually night schools. I would suggest that, in co-operation with the local authorities all over the Dominion, the minister should encourage the improvement of these local schools. They are now working under disabilities. The teacher can only be given a small salary and he is usually a man who has to work for his living during the day, giving perhaps three or four nights in the week to the work of teaching in these schools. The schools have done excellent work in encouraging our young men. It is to be stated with pride that, whereas twenty or thirty years ago we have very few of our own young men acting as mine managers in Nova Scotia, and we had to get managers from Scotland, England and Wales, the condition is entirely reversed now. Although we have ten times as many managers now as then, we have scarcely any person in charge of our works except our own men who have received their education in our own schools and colleges. I hope the minister will find it convenient and possible to extend this line of education to all the industries in the country.
In large manufacturing centres it is highly desirable that technical education should be introduced among the workmen, and matters so arranged that it would be an advantage to any person engaged in any class of manufacturing in this country that he or she shall have passed a course of training in some one of these schools.
I wish to point out to the minister on thing in connection with shipbuilding in Canada. Some forty years ago Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Prince Edward Island carried on a great deal of shipbuilding, largely wooden ships, but it had rather gone out of vogue and comparatively very few people were paying any attention to it. Since the war there has been a revival in shipbuilding on onr Pacific and Atlantic coasts, but the sad part of it is that in many cases it was extremely difficult to find anybody who knew anything about the building of a ship. I know of an instance in my own county where men grouped themselves together, formed a company, and started to build ships, but they found it very difficult indeed to acquire the services of an experienced shipbuilder. I think they ultimately found in Newfoundland a man who possessed the necessary qualifications. Now seeing that wooden shipbuilding and iron and steel building are pretty much along the same lines, I would suggest to the minister that broader fields of this kind should be considered and the expenditure of this money should . not be confined to . any narrow limits. Rather the greatest possible expansion should be given to our ideas in this direction, and thus put Canada on the highway to prosperity in all the lines of commercial enterprise, productiveness, and development generally, for which we are so well fitted and which the resources of the country render us so capable of undertaking.

I must congratulate the minister on taking this step and I am very pleased indeed that something is now being done to promote the spread of technical education. I have been a member of this House for some fifteen years and the subject has been discussed on several occasions, but we have been very slow in the matter of accomplishment. If there is a criticism to make it is that the resolution does not apply to the current year.
It applies to the current year.

Then I withdrew my criticism in that regard. Another point I wish to make is that the Federal Government should not tie up the provinces in matters affecting technical education where the business can better be conducted by a Provincial Government and the whole responsibility thrown upon it. The present administration seems to be working out a policy by which the local legislatures will be tied up to the Federal authority. That would appear to be evident in connection with the housing and road-building policies and the present technical education scheme. I think it would be more in the interest of the country if, when there is money that can be spared for local purposes, that money should be given at once in the form of a subsidy to the local Government and the responsibility thrown upon it of making the expenditure in the best interest of the province.
In regard to the proposal which we are now considering, a good deal will depend upon the administration. In the province from which I come domestic science and manual training are taught in the main public schools; and in the mining districts as my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) has said, we have had for a good many years schools for training miners in the technical part of their education. Then in the industrial centres there are night schools and other schools where boys can take a course in technical education. The question I want to raise is whether the money expended in various directions on technical schools by a province will be counted in the total estimate of the amount to be contributed by it? Do I understand that the proposition we are considering means that if $100,000 is contributed by the Federal Government to a province, the latter must put up an equal amount? If I am correct in that, then, for example, in the province of Nova Scotia, where some of the schools giving instruction in manual training, domestic science, and so forth, are supported by the town or municipality, will the money so furnished be counted in the $100,000 that will be contributed by the province? As I say a good deal depends on the administration, and if the minister insists that the money contributed by the province shall be devoted entirely to what is called in a narrow sense technical education, it will make a great difference in the .administration of the Act.

It will be noticed from the resolution that in determining the grant payable to any province no account

shall be taken of any liabilities or expenditure incurred by the province for the acquiring of land, the erection or improvement of any buildings or the supplying of furnishings or equipment for any technical educational institution established in the province prior to the first of April, 1919. That is, no account shall be taken of capital expenditures heretofore incurred by the province.
I am not referring to capital expenditures.

I am just coming to the point which was raised by the hon. gentleman. In so far as the scheme generally is concerned it is not proposed that the Federal Government .should grant any assistance to the provinces for carrying on domestic science, vocational training, nature study, manual training, or any of that class of work in our elementary schools. Courses in such subjects are now given by the various provinces of Canada in all the elementary schools; that instruction is going on throughout the country. For example, in the rural schools of Saskatchewan they are now teaching cooking and sewing, and the farm boys are taught manual training and kindred subjects. Some reports were furnished me the other day by one of our inspectors who looks after certain foreign-speaking districts in the province, and the class of work that is carried on even amongst our foreign-bom ' people in the rural portions of Saskatchewan, and the success which has been achieved, is really amazing. Practically the the same sort of instruction is being oarried on in all the urban centres of Canada; and the provinces have come to recognize their responsibility for these new forms of elementary school work. So it is not intended, under this resolution, or under the Bill to be founded upon it, to take into account at all whatever expenditures are made by the provinces in that direction.
I am speaking of the education that is given to the boys and girls in the ordinary elementary schools, or even in the ordinary high schools, because certain phases of that work are carried on in the high schools as well.
There is another branch of what is referred to by the leader of the Opposition; that is, certain industrial classes that are held not for teaching youths or children, but young men who are actually working in industries, and some of the provinces

have embarked on a very large programme in that regard. This Bill will be administered by the Minister of Labour. I have had a good many conversations with him, and he has in mind that that is one of the most important features of the work to be done. While we must have our technical educational institutions, that is, the large institutions thoroughly equipped in order to give the technical training associated with those institutions, we cannot bring that type of institution to everybody, and his idea is that wherever it is possible to give workmen who are in their ordinary employment the benefit of technical education by bringing instructors to them in order to increase their efficiency, that should be done. Because, after all, the results that can be secured under measures of this kind are not entirely attributable to large buildings and costly equipment. More, in my judgment, depends upon the instructor than upon anything else, and as far as possible the moneys provided by means of these grants should be used for the purpose of securing proper instructors and training them. In the United States -where they have given a great deal of attention to the subject, more so than we have here, and where they have made far greater advances than we have-under, I think, the Smith-Hughes Act of 1917, they provide for a co-operative scheme with the States, and the grants are payable entirely for the purpose of providing salaries for instructors and for training them, because they realize, as I am sure we realize more and more every day, that that is really the heart of the whole situation. We must have the men who can give proper instruction in the various classes of subjects to be taught. I do not know whether I have met the hon. gentleman's point or not.

With regard to the mixed system which we have in our province, part of the money that supports those technical schools is contributed by the provincial governmeent and part by the towns. Will that money count in the total for the province? I see no reason why it should not.

It is not proposed that any contribution made by a municipality for the establishment or maintenance of one of these institutions shall be taken into account. ThAt is a matter of arrangement betweeen the provincial Government and the local authorities. It is proposed that our grant shall equal the amount that is
expended by the province. What arrangement it cares to make with the municipality is a matter of its own concern.

I would ask the minister whether the exact terms of these resolutions have been the subject of discussion with the provincial governments; and, if so, whether they are acceptable to those governments. Of course, I know the scheme can only apply to any province after the Governor in Council has approved of the agreement entered into with the province. But sometimes we may propose something, which, however good its intention, the provincial governments may not be able to take advantage of. I am afraid there is something of that in out efforts to aid highways. But in this case my question is whether the provincial governments have been made aware of these resolutions and have intimated that they will be satisfactory.
I would like to emphasize the point raised by my hon. friend (Mr. J. H. Sinclair). I was about to ask the same question-whether the department here would insist upon limiting the expenditure to the sum paid by the Government of the province directly, or whether it might be expended under the educational system of the province, perhaps not by the provincial government but by the municipalities. The mere fact that the work is done by the municipalities does not condemn it if it is technical education. I suppose when we have the Bill before us my hon. friend will give us a better definition of what he considers is technical education under the Act, and perhaps until the Bill is brought down it will be just as well to reserve criticism. But it will be necessary to have a definite understanding on these two points: first, as to what is the technical education to which this money may be applied; and, second, if technical education is carried on in any province by arrangement between the provincial government and the municipalities why should not that count in. I only ask my hon. friend to give it consideration in framing the Bill. I have in mind the mining schools in Nova Scotia to which my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition referred. They have been doing good work in that province and they are strictly technical institutions. I have no doubt that it will be possible to adapt this measure to the conditions existing in the different provinces.
At six o'clock the Committee took recess.



After Recess.
The Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, it has long been expected that some action would be taken in the matter dealt with by this resolution. Some time ago a commission of inquiry went fully into the subject of technical education and industrial training, and the report which it submitted received the admiration of all countries. At last the recommendations of this report are being put into effect. In New Brunswick we have been very much in need of technical education in all its branches, and I have no doubt that the Provincial Government will co-operate in every possible way to make this measure a success.
Such matters as technical education, highways, and so on may be dealt with by the Dominion Government in such a way as to constitute an infringement of provincial rights. I have always been an advocate of provincial rights, and I believe that there is no stronger or more sincere advocate of provincial rights than the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Calder) who presents this resolution. I remember that in 1913, when a Highways Bill was proposed which would have curtailed provincial rights, no Provincial Government was more pronounced in its opposition to that proposed infringement of provincial rights than the Government of which my hon. friend was a member at that time. My hon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Sifton) was also a strong advocate of provincial rights. The provinces of Ganada are all examples of just and progressive administration of provincial affairs. Nova Scotia has certainly been a worthy example of the proper administration of provincial matters. Quebec is noted all over the Dominion as a province which is strong in its administration of local affairs. Ontario is	also	strong and	determined in its provincial administration, and the provinces of the West have been properly administering the matters which come under their jurisdiction. I have always contended that the subsidies paid to the provinces by the Dominion are insufficient. Last autumn when the provincial Premiers met in conference at Ottawa a demand was made for an increase of the subsidies paid to the provinces. I would have been pleased had that increase been granted, and the provinces thus been	put	in a	better position to look after such things as housing and highways and technical education.

The provinces have not been able to make progress in these matters because of the lack of means. Some of the provinces have taken these matters up, however, and have dealt with them to the extent of their ability to do so. In Quebec there are a great many technical institutions which are a credit to the province and would be a credit to any province.
I congratulate the minister upon bringing forward such a measure as this; he has done one good thing in this Government, if he has done nothing else. I hope that with the knorvledge that he has of the ability of the provinces to conduct their own affairs; with the confidence that he has in the men administering the affairs of the provinces, and with his solicitude for the maintenance of provincial rights, he will be able to impose his will upon his colleagues in the same direction in the future. I hope that the Government will not bring forward any further measure which may have a tendency to infringe upon provincial rights. Had the provinces ' the means to do so, they would deal with these matters according to their own judgment and with all the ardour which they have displayed in other matters. It is time the attention of the Government was directed to the tendency of the Federal authority to encroach upon provincial rights. The Minister of Immigration, as I have said, was certainly a great "provincial righter" when he was in the Provincial Government, and his transfer to the Federal Government certainly has not changed his principles in that regard.

The question which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Turgeon) has just raised is a very large one; it goes very much beyond the provisions of this resolution or of the Bill to be founded upon it. 1 thoroughly concur in the view that he expresses. It is very unfortunate that the relationship between the Federal Government and the provinces has not been so established that the provinces can carry on the work assigned to them under our constitution. For many years they have been pleading lack of funds, and in my judgment there is a great deal to be said in favour of that plea. As to matters of education, highways, and things of that character, there is no doubt in my mind that, the provinces should be left to carry on the work which, under the British North America Act, they were evidently intended to carry on. However, the question of the adjustment of the subsidies paid to the provinces is a very large one; probably it

will be some years before it is definitely settled. One or two slight adjustments have been made since Confederation. I think all the provinces to-day take the ground that the arrangement is a very unsatisfactory one from their point of view, having regard to the many changes that have taken place since 1867.
The hon. member is not quite right when he says that at the conference of provincial premiers and representatives last autumn, a general request was made for enlarged provincial subsidies. At that conference the question of the transfer to the Western Provinces of their natural resources came up for consideration, and in connection with that matter it was suggested that if the Western Provinces received their natural resources, the other provinces should receive increased subsidies.
I am not going to debate the question now, but generally speaking, I thoroughly concur in the view set forth by my hon. friend that if an arrangement could be made whereby the provinces could receive larger subsidies it would be an advantage if they were allowed to carry on and administer those local matters which it was intended by the British North America Act they should carry on. But I think it will be some time before an agreement is reached between the federal and the provincial authorities on this subject.

I have listened with a great, deal of interest to my hon. friend, and I think his remarks are quite timely. Yet I do not Delieve, as the minister has stated, that in the resolution there is any infringement of provincial rights. As I have on two occasions moved resolutions praying the Government to give effect to the report published by the commissioners on technical education, without, however, carrying conviction, I am rather pleased to see that today the Government is giving effect in part to that very able report. Of course, when the subject of education is brought before the federal House grave problems are found to be involved. But in those debates to which I have referred I endeavoured to draw a distinction between technical education as such and education in the sense in which it is understood generally and which makes between this Parliament and the local legislatures such a cleavage of opinion. Constitutionally, of course, the Federal Parliament cannot deal with matters of education.
As regards technical education, it would be playing on words to suggest that the
question as it presents itself constitutes an infringement on the provincial powers witn regard to the larger issue of education, because we have already in this Parliament provided, for instance, by the erection of the military college at Kingston, education in connection with military matters, which are under Dominion jurisdiction. We have in another sense provided education in matters of agriculture, which is a question which comes concurrently under both provincial and Dominion jurisdiction. I was always of opinion that in connection with trade and industry this Parliament was justified in promoting the cause of technical education. Altuough some of the provinces have, during the last twenty-five or thirty years, taken quite a lead, yet all credit must be given to the little province by the sea, Nova Scctia, which many years ago was the pioneer in matters of technical education. That is the reason why the men from Nova Scotia have so distinguished themselves not only in the political field, but in the industrial and educational lines throughout the Dominion. It is because in that little province, there is a thorough and most effective system of education, and technical education is not the least feature of the larger system. I am proud to say that Ontario has gone pretty far in matters of technical education, and of late the province from which I come has accomplished considerably in that field. We have in Quebec at present what I consider the banner institution as regards technical education. Those who have visited in Montreal the technical school on Sherbrooke street will not hesitate to say that it is the finest institution of the kind in Canada and one of the finest in America. I have not the statistics at hand, but I know from the report of the Provincial Secretary that the establishment of that school in our province has produced very satisfactory results.
I will give only a solitary instance ot what has been accomplished by that school. Four years ago I met at Drummondville a farmer's son who had just received his degree at the Technical Institute at Montreal. It was at the time when young men were asked to help towards the production of munitions, and technical experts were needed in various establishments to promote that production. That young French Canadian, having received a letter of introduction from your humble servant, went to one of the munition manufacturers in Montreal, and inside of six weeks he was at the head of that establishment. He was

not more than twenty-one years old and was already receiving a very large salary. There I had a concrete example of what technical education can accomplish.
I know that, as a rule, speaking for my province, while the men of Quebec have an ingrained intelligence for industrial work, they have lacked that last finishing touch which technical education will develop. In the last five years there has been quite a change in this connection, and our young men have become leaders of industry. I have that from no less an authority than Lord Shaughnessy himself. The Canadian Pacific, as hon. members are aware, employs a large number of technical experts in its shops throughout Canada, and I know that in the district of Montreal, the young men who have passed through the technical school are now getting large salaries and steady employment from our railway companies and large industrial firms. Therefore, I see with pleasure the determination qf the Government to do something practical towards promoting the cause of technical education throughout Canada. We all know that the success of Germany notably, and also of the United States, and of the Mother Country, in industrial fields, is due chiefly to the high technical education which has been spread throughout the industrial districts of those countries.
Now that this unfortunate war is over, and now that, as we were told this afternoon, our country must produce not only in the field of agriculture, which is the basic industry of Canada, but also in the industrial lines, the more we spend wisely on technical education the greater will be the part that our production will play in the commerce of the world.
There is only one thing I regret, and it is the fact .that- this legislation comes 'so late. In connection with this matter and others too, the Government should have started its programme during the war. Its present measure seems to be rather tardy. However, "better late than never," and I shall vote with pleasure to carry on this policy. I said a moment ago that I appreciated the remarks made toy my hon. friend from Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon) in regard to provincial autonomy. But I believe that there are safeguards in the legislation which is being promoted by the hon. Minister of Immigration and Colonization. Subsection (f) of the resolution provides that every province receiving a grant shall furnish the minister with the necessary evidence to show that the grants paid are expended for technical edu-
['Mr. Lemieux.]
cation as provided by the proposed legislation. This is a safeguard for both the province and the Dominion. The Dominion Government has the right to see that such moneys as are advanced are spent for the object intended, and that object alone the same as in the case of the moneys given to the provinces for the promotion of agriculture. A grant is made yearly .to the various provinces and the Federal authorities exercise a moderate control of the same nature as that now proposed, I am quite sure that my hon. friend (Mr. Gaidar), knowing the several provinces as he does, will have no difficulty in coming .to an understanding with the provincial authorities, and that there will be between the Provincial Governments and the Dominion Government an entente cordiale on this particular subject. As I said a moment ago, I do not wish to delay the Committee, but I desire to express my sincere approval of this policy of promoting technical education in the various provinces of the Dominion. The report of the commission appointed in 1910 to investigate the question, and which was tabled many sessions ago, is a most interesting one. Indeed, it is creditable to Canada that such a report should have been published. The report itself is too bulky to be properly read with any expedition. It needs to be studied and inwardly digested, and to do it adequate justice would take time. But Professor Robertson has prepared a synopsis which ought to be read by every member of the Committee^ He goes much further than the question of technical education in industrial amd trade matters. He wants technical institutes for the fishermen and the farmers, and I suppose the day will come when the Government will give effect to the views expressed by Professor Robertson and thus implement the conclusions arrived at by the Commissioners who prepared that highly interesting report.

The hon. member for M.aisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) said he thought there would be no difficulty in coming to an agreement with the several provinces. When the Bill is before the House it will be seen that it is so worded as to be quite elastic in that respect, and I think that is only proper. In a country such as Canada, where varying conditions exist and with the many industries that we have, it was felt that the law should not be too rigid, and that the question as to the manner in which these moneys should be used should

largely be made the subject of an agreement between the federal and the provincial authorities. Personally, I think that principle is a sound one and I have not the slightest doubt, from the discussions that took place at the conference last fall, that there will be no difficulty whatever in coming to a proper working arrangement with each of the provinces. We shall have an opportunity of considering all the details of the Bill in Committee, and unless there is some other matter in connection with this resolution requiring explanation,
I would suggest that the resolution be allowed to go through, with the opportunity for further discussion in view.

Before the resolution is passed, I would call the attention of the minister to the system of distribution of this money as here set forth. Before six o'clock, when I was speaking on the matter, I had not an opportunity of carefully reading the resolution. Since then I have read it, and I submit to the minister that the method by which he proposes to distribute the money to the provinces is not in harmony with the system of free school education which has been established in nearly every province. In the old days poor children could not be educated because their fathers could not pay for their education. We largely surmounted that difficulty by establishing free schools, and perhaps our own province was the pioneer in this respect. There is in the smaller and perhaps poorer provinces just as much talent, ingenuity and ambition among the young people as in the larger and more wealthy and populous provinces. Now, if there is a poor province that cannot put up money for technical education it will receive none of this grant, and in any case it will not get any more than dollar for dollar on what it contributes. I ask the minister seriously to consider the question of making some proper provision in this respect. The idea is to help the genius of our people in the way of technical education, and there should be nothing to prevent the minister from distributing this money in such a manner as will effect that purpose. If a province has no money and cannot contribute for technical education $10,000,	$20,000 or $30,000, or whatever
amount may be sufficient to inaugurate the system, its people will not be helped at all. That was not the method in connection with the road grants. Twenty million dollars is supposed to be distributed to the provinces
for good roads. I understand that a lump sum is granted each province and the balance of the vote is divided among the provinces according to population. In that case the small province benefits fairly well with others that are more wealthy and populous.
lln this case, the province will not get more than it puts up. Take a sfnall province like Prince Edward Island with its very excellent talent. There is no province in Canada that has better men along technical, industrial and educational lines than the little province of Prince Edward Island. But when it comes to putting up thousands of dollars for the purpose of education, I am afraid it has not the revenue. The same thing to a great extent is true of the newer provinces such as British Columbia, and the result is that the bulk of this money will go to the two big, wealthy provinces of Ontario and Quebec. They are very much better off and better equipped for carrying out technical education without any help than the smaller provinces. I wish seriously to -remind the minister and the Government of this particular part of the scheme and to urge them to see that nothing is allowed to happen that will defeat the purpose of the vote.

If this resolution is
adopted I think we might take it for granted that the principle that the hon. gentleman has referred to might be left for further consideration. Both in regards to agricultural aid and highways there is a provision whereby some of the provinces get a special grant. That is not done in this case but it is worth considering whether or not the same principle should be applied here. If the resolution is agreed to I think we could have an understanding that when the Bill is before us that principle is still open for discussion.	*
Mr. LEMIEUX That is, that a minimum will be fixed?
Yes.

I hope the minister will not forget the suggestion I made in relation to industrial towns. There are industrial towns that are very anxious to have technical schools and they have levied a tax of a certain amount to establish and maintain these schools. If the province is not in a position to furnish the money, I see no reason why the towns should not be allowed to assess themselves to assist the province in establishing techni-

cal schools or why the money contributed should not count in the amount contributed by the province.

I will bear that point in mind. I think it is well worth consideration. Let -me put it in concrete form. In the city of Peterborough, for instance, they are desirous of establishing a technical school. They are prepared to put up the necessary building, provide the equipment, and so on. The provincial government may not feel justified in giving a grant towards this institution but the local people are prepared to put up the money to take care of the capital expenditure and maintenance. Under the law, no grant would be available for that institution unless the province contributed to it. It is worth while to consider whether or not this grant should be made available if the municipalities, instead of the province, are prepared to assist a scheme of this kind.
Mr. PETER MoGIBBON: To my mind there is a possibility of this money being practically all consumed by large cities like Toronto and Hamilton .and that towns even as large as Peterborough will not participate in it to any great degree. Technical education, like education of any kind, is something that should be scattered broadcast throughout the country and it should be made possible for boys and girls in every part of the province to attend these schools if they so desire. It does not seem to me that there are any arrangements made whereby that can be worked out.
Mr. (CALDER: The question as to where these institutions shall be established and what money shall be expended in connection with them is all a matter of agreement between the provincial government and the Minister of Labour.
Mr. PETER MoGIBBON: I quite understand that hut the point I desired to make was that under the present provincial system that is practically what happens. When the Dominion Government is stepping into the field and giving $10,000,000, I think there should be some guarantee that this money shall not be concentrated in the large cities, because they Only supply a small percentage of the people.

What are the reasons for the provisions in paragraph 4 and paragraph 5, subsections (lb) and (c)? If the Dominion is prepared to make the grant that is provided for by this resolution it 
will be well to consider carefully the provisions that (these paragraphs seem to make. Take a municipality like the town of Renfrew. They are considering the advisability of erecting' a new collegiate institute in conjunction with which there is to be a technical school. They have arrived at a difficult point in their -consideration of the proposal. The difficulty is that, whereas the municipality pays the entire cost of constructing the building, the pupils -coming from outside the municipality pay nothing towards the cost. Over 55 per cent of the pu-pils -come from outside the municipality, and it is- considered very unfair that the municipality should provide the building and equipment for the education of pupils who come from the outside. Therefore, it is contended they should receive assistance towards the -building and equipment of the institution that provides education facilities for children who are not in the municipality. They have made application to the Provincial Government for assistance towards the erection of that building. I would like to know if it is the intention of this Government to allow a part of the grant, if this resolution is carried, for a specific case of that kind or must it be used only for the maintenance of the institution, no part of the money to be provided being used for the erection of the building?

Under clause 3 of section 5 provision is- made to the effect that not more than 25 per cent of the grant payable to any province may be used for capital expenditure. Just where and how these moneys shall be used for capital expenditure will be a matter of agreement between the province and the Federal Government.

Why make an exception in applying a part of the grant to institutions which are already in existence? For instance, I understand, there is in Montreal a splendid institution in operation and doing excellent work. Why not provide in section 4 that part of this money shall be applied towards the improvement or extension of that institution? As I read the section in its present form that cannot be done.

As I explained this afternoon, the purpose of this grant is to provide for new work, not to take care of old expenditure. The whole amount would be eaten up -by past expenditures if we were to adopt the hon. gentleman's suggestion.

What we want to do is to provide for new ' technical institutions and not take care of expenditures which have been already made.
But suppose in the case of the institution referred to it - is desired to extend the building?

There is nothing here that will prevent a grant being made providing it is to be applied to an extension. This provision only prohibits using these grants for past expenditures and does not relate to new outlays.

Then the Bill to be
founded on this resolution will make provision for that?

Yes.
Besolution reported, read the first and second time and concurred in.
Mr. Calder thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill 131, for the promotion of Technical Education in Canada.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
