Does the minister find that he has any applications from returned soldiers for the positions of lock men?
Mr. J. D. ElBID: All appointments of employees on these canals are made by the Civil Service Commission, and so far as I know only returned soldiers are appointed. I have insisted that in every case where returned soldiers are available, and can fill the positions, they are to be appointed. Up to the present time there has been no trouble in filling these positions with returned soldiers. The positions are suitable for returned men who have been wounded and are only capable of light outside work. It is only when a vessel locks through the canals that the men really are employed, and it is not hard work. So far the men have appreciated it.
In the case of three or four applicants for one vacancy, is there any system by which the department makes its selections from returned men?

The chief engineer
makes application and the appointments are made by the Civil (Service Commission.
I have never interfered. But I did suggest to the engineer-at least, I have asked for it in my own constituency, and I think it is a good policy to follow-that he select men in this way:	The man that should
have the first opportunity of taking the position should be a wounded man who is married and has a family; the (Second choice should be a married man who has served overseas for a certain length of time and has not been wounded; the next a single man who has been wounded at the front; the fourth a single man who has fought tat the front and has not been wounded. The Commission have been able to find men who have families, and I think a man who left his family of small children and went overseas and then returns wounded should have the first choice of any position we can give him.

I think the system oi selection set forth by the minister is fair.
If there is no other way of selection, I would even suggest that the length of service should count. In the case of two men one with three years' service at the front in the trenches and another with only a year's service, all other things being equal,
I would give the preference to the man with the longer service. In this 9 p.m. part of the country where the canals are close to the depart-

ment I suppose there is closer supervision than is possible in remote districts. In the case of the St. Peter's canal-the only canal we have, as far as I remember, in the Maritime Provinces-I have heard complaints that the selection of men to fill vacancies was made by the lockmaster rather in a partisan way, and of course that is not the intention of the minister-
Oh, no.

-nor of the department. I have received letters from that part of the country saying that the lockmaster was prevailed upon to make appointments which were not consistent with the merits of the applicants.

I understand that the Civil Service Commission advertise in almost every case. Possibly they may have asked the lockmaster for information as to the qualifications of applicants. I do not know what means they take for obtaining such information. The main point I wish to emphasize is that I asked the chief engineer when he is making the applications, *that if there are men in that particular locality who have been at the front and have been wounded and probably are not able to do any hard work, such men should get the preference. It is not a question of politics; I would not stand for that for one minute. A man might be overseas for four years and not get wounded, while another man might be over for only two years and come back wounded and incapable of doing other work. In that case I would feel that the man who is really unable to perform other work, but would be able to till one of these positions, should be appointed. I have had them hold positions open in my own constituency until the men came back. I remember a case of a returned man with a wife and three children who was shot through the arm, rendering the limb stiff so that he could not do any hard work, but he was quite qualified for one of these canal positions. Of course, in a case like that he would get the preference over returned men who were not wounded, and were capable of undertaking any kind of work.
At all events, we are employing only returned soldiers. If others have slipped in, it is without my knowledge. Further, we have been making places for returned' soldiers by letting out men who have other means and are able to get along without doing this work.

What I meant was
that, other things being equal, there being no other means of differentiating between two men who were applying, I suppose the question of military service would come in.

The hon. member will understand that we do not know anything about the man who has the position until he comes with his certificate from the Civil Service Commission. There was a case in my own county where a married man with a family and a single man were applicants for a position, and the single man got the certificate. All we can do in a case of that kind is to bring the matter to the attention of the Civil Service Commission, in which case the commission might reconsider it.

I must say that I
have heard no complaint in this regard except the one I have mentioned. I suggest that the minister cause an inquiry to be made as to how many men were put on the St. Peter's canal, and how they were selected, or by whom they were recomended.

I shall be glad to do
that.
How is a returned soldier to apply for a position, say, on the Intercolonial railway? Suppose he wants to be a cleaner in a roundhouse, or a brakeman, to whom is he to make application?

To the superintendent
of the division. As my hon. friend knows, the Government railways do not come under the Civil Service Commission. The President, Mr. Hanna, thoroughly understands the policy to be followed in that regard; returned soldiers must have the preference in all cases where they can be obtained. Of course, the selections must be made a little more carefully for a railway than, perhaps, for other branches of the public service. The position to be filled might be one of responsibility, where life was at stake. But now that the soldiers are practically all home you can get a returned man for almost any position. So far, I have been able to do so.
I understood that there was a mechanical officer at Moncton who looked after all applications for positions in the mechanical department in the whole of the eastern division.

Of course, the superintendent may hand the application over to the head of the particular department in which the man wishes to be employed, and there his application would be considered. Many applications come to me from persons who do not understand that the department has nothing to do with these appointments. These applications are forwarded to Mr. Hanna, who has them sent to the proper officials.

I have been asked whether returned soldiers take precedence in the matter of appointments to others holding temporary positions on the railway, and I could not give a definite answer. Let us assume that in one of the roundhouses, or on a particular section of the road, a number of men are temporarily employed and. a returned soldier is anxious to get one of these positions; is it the policy of the Government to make room for the returned soldier by letting one of those men off?

The policy is this: Wherever a new .man is taken on a returned soldier must have the preference. But the brotherhoods insist upon their men being promoted; they will not allow a man to be dismissed to make room for some one else.
Then you make a distinction between permanent employees and temporary employees in that matter?

Well, I could not say as to that; I would have to take that up with the officials. But all men must be employed temporarily at first, no matter what the positions are. The hon. member probably refers to men who are taken on for a month or two months. In all cases, whether the position is one to be filled for a day, a week, or two or three weeks, the returned soldier has the preference. But if there is a vacancy in a roundhouse, and if there is a man below who belongs to the union, he would be promoted to the position vacateu, and his position would, in turn, be filled by a returned soldier. But you have to follow out the rules of the union; you cannot deprive a man of his promotion.

Then I understand that if there are some temporary employees in a roundhouse and a returned soldier asks for one of the positions, if those men desire to stay there the minister will not interfere with them, but when there is a vacancy a position may be given to the returned sol dier? That is not doing very much for the soldier.

Pa. I of this item is $42,500 for statistical officers. 1 understood that when the Dominion Bureau of .Statistics was organized the collection of statistics by the different departments was to be abandoned. If I am correct in that, why the provision for these statistical officers?

That item has been there for a good many years. The statistics are forwarded to the Board of Railway Commissioners and to the Bureau of Statistics, which is under the Department ol Trade and Commerce.
Some years ago these men.used to be called collectors of canal tolls, and now that canal tolls are abolished, the men are called statistical officers. On the Rideau canal, for instance, we have a man here who issues passes for vessels going from Ottawa to Kingston, and there is another man at Kingston. Vessels have to have passes to go through the canals. In getting a pass the captain of a vessel has to give these men a report as to the cargo, whether it is light or heavy, the name of the vessel, and other information. This appropriation is to pay these men and others. Our statistics branch has practically disappeared, there remaining only four or five of the officials, and no more statistics will be printed and circulated by the Department of Railways and Canals.

The same amount oi money was appropriated last year for the same purpose, and I understood then that, if not all, at least a major portion of the work would be done by this new Bureau of Statistics. Such work as the minister has referred to should be done by the local men at the port of entry. These men should be capable of doing the work as well as the collecting, thus dispensing with the appointment of statistical officers for that particular work. The work cannot be very exacting, and any man of ordinary business capacity should be able to keep a record of vessels going through the canals, the tonnage and so forth, and forward it to the Bureau of Statistics,

I was reading somewhere the other day of an inquiry in which a former member of this House, Mr. German, I think, gave his opinion as tO' the enlargement of this canal.
I do not know whether the minister saw the interview or statement it was to the effect that the money expended upon the enlargement of this canal to a capacity much greater than the navigable capacity at each end of the canal was really money expended to no purpose, that the department is now deepening the canal to 22 feet on the sills, that for miles and miles at either end there is only sufficient depth of water to accommodate a vessel with a draught of 8 or 9 feet at the outside, and that it may be many years before there can be any return to the country for this large expenditure upon a certain section in the middle of the system. This is like a man who forges a chain 100 feet in length; he makes a certain section of the links very strong and' stout and the rest of the links very weak. The old saying is that the strength of the chain is the strength of the weakest link. Will the minister explain what good purpose that enlarged section serves when the rest of the waterway from Montreal to Kingston is not sufficiently deep to carry a vessel of the size for which he is providing in the enlargement of the Welland canal?

I did not see the interview with Mr. German but perhaps I might explain what I think he refers to. In the first place, in order to construct this canal from lake Ontario to lake Erie, it was divided into eight sections. For four of them the contract was given out some years ago. These are right in the middle of the canal. They are lock work. The building of the locks will take twice as long as the other work. The intention was to commence the other sections when this work was about half through so that all would

be completed at the same time. Probably Mr. German was expressing the view that when this work in the middle of the canal was completed it would be no use because the ends had not been completed. I;f the work at the ends were going on now all the work would be completed at the same time, so that a vessel could go right through to Montreal. The other work to be done is more like dredging, and it will have to be completed when times get normal and when we get down to prices which are fairly reasonable. The prices of material and labour are so high that I think we should go as slowly as possible. It is only to give employment to people who are out of work that we are proceeding with this work at the present time. There is another point that the hon. member may have-referred to. Perhaps Mr. German said that we were making this 30 feet in depth when probably the waterway above has a less depth of water. I do not know whether that is the fact or not but I want to point ou't that in constructing this canal we are making the depth greater than that of the St. Lawrence canals at the present time. We are making it 25 or 30 feet .so that a vessel can go to Kingston or Prescott. She could not go on to Montreal because there is only a depth of 14 feet on the sills in 'the St. Lawrence canals. Still people may say that you would not want a greater depth for many years. When the Welland canal was built first it was a 9-foot canal and the reports of the department said that they expected it would last for thirty years. Just about the time the work was completed they were in the same position as when they started out, for larger vessels had been constructed. They then deepened the canal to 12 'feet. The records of the department will show that Mr. Page, who was then the chief engineer of the department, stated that a 12-foot canal was good for thirty years. Before they got through with that 12-foot canal they found they were in about the same position as before,-ten-thousand-ton vessels are operating on these western lakes. In the early days the vessels that ran between Chicago, Kingston and Montreal were vessels of 1,000 or 1,500 tons. Then they got up to 2,500 or 3,000 tons, and they have been increasing until now the vessels that operate from Lake Superior down to Buffalo are 10,000 or 12,000-ton vessels, capable of carrying 400,000 bushels of wheat. The intention is that these same vessels shall go through the canal and on to Kingston at least. Port Colborne, which is at the head of the AVellatod canal, is only

a few miles from Buffalo. These vessels operate from Lake Superior to Buffalo. There is no reason why they should not go through this canal and on to Kingston. The ground is taken by a number of people who are well posted on this matter that the Welland canal should not be proceeded with. The minister has not dealt with that question. I was very much impressed with the speech of the Finance Minister this afternoon regarding the financial condition of the country, which everybody admits is very serious. I would be surprised to learn that Mr. German ever made any such statement as that which is attributed to him in the circular which has been, just read. Let me say that we are not starting a new work; the sum of $16,000,000 has already been expended on the project. It was commenced several years ago, but operations were suspended owing to the war. The enlargement of the Welland canal is not a new undertaking; the commencement of the canal dates back to fifty or sixty years ago, beginning first with a depth of nine feet, then twelve feet, and now an even deeper waterway is proposed. Reference has been made to the amount of grain that passed through the canal in the course of a year. We are not dealing with a canal capable merely of carrying the quantity of grain that passes through it in one year; this canal is being constructed to take care of the grain and the products originating in the West for many years to come. The grain from Western Canada that is transported to Liverpool to-day goes in large 10,000-ton vessels, 'by the American route to

There is no question about it, a very large saving in transportation charges will be effected by the improvement of our system of canals. The trip is probably twenty-four hours longer from Port Colborne to Kingston, and they may charge a small amount for that extra day's operation of the steamer. 60,000	or 65,000 bushels would continue to operate between Port Colborne and Montreal, a distance of probably four hundred miles.

terested in it and are taking it up with great energy with a view of routing their traffic to Montreal or to the Atlantic instead of having to tranship it at Buffalo for conveyance to New York. The advantage to the American side of the river, if they canalize the St. Lawrence, would he that these 10,000-ton or 8,000-ton vessels- and the latter is quite a large tonnage now-crossing the Atlantic will load at Liverpool or at any other port and return straight to Chicago, Duluth or Buffalo. The benefit would accrue to the big freighters; there would be no benefit to the small freighters, because the present accommodation is sufficient for them. The statement is made by this gentleman, who knows the grain trade intimately, that the big freighters prefer to discharge their cargo at Port Col-
10 p.m. borne because they can get a return cargo. How is the minister going to get over that? If he cannot get the big freighters to come down to Kingston, then his big canal will be no good to any body.

Here is another advantage of boats coming to Kingston instead of Port Colborne. When the Soo canal was constructed on the same lines as the Welland and other canals-as it originally was -a vessel carrying about 65,000 bushels was the largest that could proceed from Port Arthur or Fort William to Buffalo, and the rate was about five cents a bushel. Immediately the Soo canal became available for boats of 10,000 tons, the rates were cut down to one and-a-half to two cents a bushel. That was a great advantage to those who were selling their grain in the West. The same thing applies on a vessel now from Port Colborne to Montreal. A vessel would probably get two or three cents a bushel between those points, whereas the rate from Kingston to Montreal is one and-a-half cents-they would probably charge three and-a-half cents a bushel; whereas the large freighter of 10,000 tons would probably bring that cargo from Port Colborne to Kingston at half a cent a bushel on account of the large quantity and the time taken-only one day. I think there is no doubt that if we want to hold our traffic for our own ports through our own country, the only possible water route is through the Welland canal and the St. Lawrence river. Then again, if we want to give to the people of the West the advantages of getting cheap transportation between- Port Arthur or Fort William and Montreal so that they will get that much more for their grain, the only way is through t'he Welland canal and the St. Lawrence river to Montreal. I have no doubt of that. But at the same time I make a proposition to the minister by which the Western grain men would get their grain to Montreal absolutely free. If he would save this $50,000,000 and put it out at 5 per

cent he would have two and a half million dollars a year, and that would pay all the freight on grain from Fort William to Montreal, and we would keep our $50,000,000 for future investment. That is the proposition made to the minister, and I do not think he has met it.

Does my hon. friend
mean that the grain would be shipped by rail from Port Arthur to Montreal?

I hope, and I think every member of the Committee believes, that our great Northwest will be filled up in the years to come, and we want facilities to carry the grain between these points at the cheapest possible rates. That grain went via Buffalo and New York because the waterway between those points hfjs been enlarged, and the rate is so much cheaper than it is between Port Colburne and Montreal. If we had the new Welland canal constructed and the St. Lawrence route improved you could go from Port Colborne to Montreal in twenty-four hours, whereas you could not go from Buffalo to New York in less than three days. I am not, in principle, opposed to the deepening of the Welland canal, although this vast expenditure was

entered upon at a time when it was said to be good policy to forego the construction of a real, national waterway, the Georgian Bay canal. All the western legislatures and all the western interests favoured the Georgian Bay canal, but for a reason which I shall not disclose it was thought better to enter upon the expenditure which is now confronting us. This Dominion has launched into many important ventures during the last twenty-five or thirty years. We sunk millions in the Trent Valley canal, and g<jt very little return. However, the Trent Valley canal is completed. And now we are undertaking this vast expenditure on the Welland canal, without any ppldcy, so to speak. The explanations given by the minister are very vague and not to the point of the able memorandum that has been distributed broadcast by the secretary of the Dominion Millers' Association. Having regard to the revelations made this afternoon by the Minister of Finance, the Government ought to be very chary about involving the Dominion in this expenditure of $3,500,000 and perhaps hundreds of millions of dollars in the future. Sensible as the project may be, good as it may be, does my hon. friend believe that it should foe entered upon now? In view of our enormous commitments-the interest charges on our war debt, the pension charges, and so on-does not he consider that it would be wise to drop even very valuable and very sensible projects? The Minister of Finance this afternoon advised Parliament to practise very strict economy. Well, is this practising economy? In view of our financial situation; in view of the fact that we shall have to make new borrowings during the present fiscal year in order to make both ends meet, is it sound and wise policy to go on with an expenditure which might well wait for a few years? When normal conditions come in a few years, Canada, being a progressive country,, will not begrudge the expenditure of such amounts as are being asked this evening. But under present circumstances, with the unrest that prevails, with the fear that financial authorities have as to the future, and with the appalling debt that is staring us in the face surely my hon. friend should postpone this work. The section of Ontario that is most interested in this work is too patriotic, too intelligent, not to realize that sacrifices

have to be made. The West has made the sacrifice as regards the Georgian Bay canal.
I remember some years ago reading in the House resolutions adopted unanimously by the Grain Growers' Associations of the West urging upon the Government the necessity of commencing work on the Georgian Bay canal. The West has made that sacrifice. We have made it in our own province, although for many years the construction of that work has been promised. This enormous expenditure will affect seriously the credit of our country. As was stated this afternoon by the Minister of Finance 'the credit of Canada must be maintained unimpaired for the commitments of the future. The mimster does not treat this matter with his usual sagacity. Parliament is already committed to very large expenditure in connection with our railway problem. By the way, the Government is expressing itself strongly in favour of Government ownership.
The other day in the other branch of this Parliament the Government, represented there by my good friend Sir James Lougheed, was not going as far as his colleagues are in this Chamber. But that is not'the que'stion and this is only an aside. What I am aiming at is this: The Government will have to spend millions and millions, not much less than $50,000,000 on the National railways for equipment to provide for deficit. Are we not experimenting enough for such a financial year as the one we are entering upon? Why should we enter upon this enormous expenditure when we can well afford to pause and wait? This is not a normal year.

As regards the Welland canal, the hon. member practically states that we are just commencing this work. This work was originated by the Government of which he was a member, and that policy was the right one to adopt.

Mr. J. D. REID; I am coming to that. There was no objection to that policy, and we proceeded with the work in normal times. The work was closed down when the war commenced. Mr. iMcKENZIE: A matter of great national importance occurs to me in Connection with this work. My conception of

ideal transportation has always been that our grain should be carried direct by rail from the point of shipment to tide water.
I suppose it can be done cheaper the other way, but it seems to me that there is considerable difficulty in handling grain when it is shifted from one kind of conveyance to another. The Minister of Railways is also the Minister of Canals and he is competing with himself. He is working up a system of canals to take traffic from his system of railways. Would it not be well to bring these two departments together and try to strike a middle course and see if the Minister of Canals could not agree with the Minister of Railways on some system by which we might have the magnificent condition in this country that a car of grain loaded at Port Arthur, or Winnipeg, or anywhere in the West could go direct to Montreal, Halifax, or St. John and be dumped straight into the ship? We are willing to spend millions and hundreds of millions of dollars on this new railroad, the Transcontinental railway. We have built a grade of railway hitherto unknown in this country for large trains to carry freight cheaper than before. It is well worth while for the minister and all of us to consider if it is not possible, even at a small loss, when we own the railroads ourselves, to carry freight by rail from point of shipment straight to the city of Montreal, say, at tidewater?

It has been a recognized fact that the carrying of grain or any freight by water can always be done more cheaply than by rail. The very fact that the Canadian Pacific railway, which is in opposition to the Canadian Government railway, carry their grain from Port Arthur to Midland or Port McNicoll on the Georgian bay and then transfer it to the rail is proof of the economy of water transportation. They take every bushel they can by vessel, and, if I remember rightly, in normal times the very best the Canadian Pacific railway could carry grain from Port Arthur to Montreal for-and they did not claim that they were making money-was 12! cents per bushel. That was at a low rate; in winter it is 22 or 22J cents. By vessel from Port Arthur to Montreal at the same time the rates were 5 or 6 cents a bushel, or at most one-half. During the season of navigation practically no grain leaves Port Arthur or Fort Williiam over rails. The Canadian Pacific railway carry their traffic in a most economical way, and it is quite evident that when they carry freight of all kinds to and from the west by vessel, from Port
Arthur and Fort William to Georgian Bay ports, and then by rail to Montreal, the reason must be that they cannot possibly compete or carry traffic on as economic a basis by rail as by water. If they could, they would not go to the expense of unloading into elevator at Port Arthur and lifting it out of the vessel at Port McNicoll and putting it on cars again. I have taken up this matter with the railway officials, who have no doubt they can prove in a very short time that there could be no successful competition in this direction. When the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Cochrane) was Minister of Railways he gave a rate of 6 cents per bushel from Armstrong, I think, or the station opposite Fort William, through to Quebec. The steamer could take the freight at Port Arthur or Fort William and take it through to Quebec at 6 cents a bushel and make money, while on every bushel of grain we carried from Armstrong to Quebec at the same time by rail we lost money.
We could not possibly compete. That was the experience we had in operating both services. I do not know that I could give any better evidence than that, but there would not be any trouble in convincing the leader of the Opposition from evidence that could be got from the Canadian Pacific, the Canadian Northern and Grand Trunk Railway Companies, which have had actual experience both by water and rail. All of these companies have their own traffic steamers.
Canals-Capital-Trent canal-construction and betterments, $1,000,000.
Towards construction of a high level bridge over the Otonabee river at Hunter street, Feter-boro, Ont., $50,0'00.

Is that in connection
with the canal?
This is for carrying on the work that is in progress there. There are several contracts that are going on.
What were your returns from the Trent canal last year?

The only items in connection with the contract work are on the Severn division of the Trent canal. The canal has been opened through from Trenton to Orillia. Two hundred thousand dollars is asked for contracts that were started when the war broke out, and we are just starting them again to keep men employed in that district. The rest is for works along the canal, including the Gilmour's siding

bridge, four works on the four divisions to cost $11,000, $7 000, $16,000, $2,000; Grand Trunk high level bridge, $5,278; Rice lake, $14,000, etc.
Will the hon. gentleman give me any idea of the movement of ships through the Trent canal last year, the salaries paid the officials, and the returns?
The Trent canal is free of tolls. It was only opened about a year ago and it is used by small craft.
How many ships passed through the canal last year?
I have not the record here. I had been under the impression that the building of the canal was really throwing money away.
Say that a little louder, please.
I say I was under that impression until I went through it last year. We spent $16,000 000 on the Trent Valley canal.
Sunk it?

We did not sink it, and I will tell the hon. gentleman why. There is quite a lot of traffic on that canal in which small craft take part, but in addition there is 150,000 horsepower of electrical energy developed and the people of the locality get 'the benefit of it. All the power used between Toronto and Kingston is supplied from the Trent river that never would otherwise have been supplied, and if you can get 150,000 horsepower with a capital investment of $16,000,000 you are getting it cheaply. Then, we have the waterway besides.
Do we sell power?
We get a rental from the plant of the Seymour Power Company. We get the same rental that the company got, and we have quite a large revenue from that.
How much do we get?

Two dollars per horsepower at the dam. There is an electrical plant there that produces 150,000 horsepower, and there will be more produced when the canal is completed to Georgian bay, and for all we will get $2 per horse-

power. We might get more than $2 but the jdea is to give the people power at the cheapest rate.
How many horsepower did we sell last year?
We sold 30,000 or 40,000 horsepower. There is a building there ready to put additional machinery in. But on account of the war during the last five years people would not put in plants.
Are there any expenditures made on account of transmission lines?

A power house and
transmission line would have to be put in by us. The Seymour Power Company have put in their own power house and we simply rent them the water-power.
There i:s a vote of $50,000 for a bridge. Would the minister tell us something aboutr that?

That is a bridge over the canal in the city of Peterborough. The bridge will cost not less than $300,000. If we built our own small bridge it would cost $50,000 or $60,000. The city wanted a high-level bridge, they proposed to spend $300,000 or $350,000 and of that amount we will pay $50,000.
How many lift locks are there on the canal?
Two; one at Peterborough and the other at Kirkfield.
I would like to understand the policy of the Government in connection with this bridge. Does the department maintain the bridge across the St. Peter's canal?

Yes, but we do not do so in this ease because this is a permanent, high level bridge. There will be no afterexpense. We simply pay $50,000 and we are through. The mayor told me that the contract would be about $350,000, and we agreed to pay $50,000 on a cost of $300,000 or over.
The minister mentioned that it was only last year that the Trent canal was opened to traffic?

It has been open for some years, but not right out into lake Ontario; it is from Orillia down through Peterborough, but that is inland. Now the

intention is to open it from lake Ontario to Georgian bay. At present you can go almost through that entire stretch, but there are yet one or two small sections to be completed which when finished will enable a steamer to travel from Montreal to Georgian bay. At the present time the steamer can only go as far as Orillia.
This $1,000,000 is partly for the extension of the canal ?
It is for the completion of the canal to the western end.
Who are the contractors?
Randolph Macdonald, or rather the York Construction Company.
That is an old name.

The old gentleman is dead; I think very likely the present contractor is his son.
Lachine Oanal, Dredging-$25,0*00.

This is for the upper end of the Lachine canal.
Soulanges Canal, Improvements-$152,000.

The sum of $75,000 in this vote is for a road along the canal. We cut off the farmers' thoroughfare by building the canal, and we now have to build this road for them.
Trent Canal, Improvements-$329,000.

This is for repairs at Bobcaygeon. The sum of $150,000 is for the construction of a new lock there on account of the dilapidated condition of the present structure. On account of the outbreak of the war the work was temporarily abandoned. I was on the spot myself last year, and the lock will really not stand any longer. Something has got to be done right away.
What is the nature of the work?

The construction of a new lock to replace the present structure which has been in existence for probably sixty years.
Welland Canal, Improvements-$25,000.
When will the Trent canal be finished ?

There are just two small
sections on the Severn river. We have not
got through with either of them, but it will only take one season if we go at the work energetically.

I want to again bring to the minister's attention the claim of an old gentleman whose name is Paradis, which means in English " Paradise." Let me remind the minister that my old friend and his old friend, Mr. Paradis, is getting on in years. He has a just claim against the Crown, which has been examined and reexamined, investigated and re-investigated, and it seems to me that it is time a decision was arrived at. The property of the dear old gentleman was destroyed by the Intercolonial many years ago, and his claim has been before the Exchequer Court and before the department. I understand there is only a question of a few thousand dollars as between Mr. Paradis and the minister. My hon. friend is convinced, I believe, that Paradis is an honest man. He has already one foot in the grave, and he would not deprive the Government of a red cent to* which he was not legally entitled. Cannot the minister, who is a young man compared with Mr. Paradis, help this old gentleman to close his eyes in peace and allow his family to receive the amount which belongs to him?

This claim came up before my predecessor and he was prepared to recommend a payment of $7,500. The amount was afterwards increased to $12,000, and the last time I took the matter up, in order to try and effect a settlement, I was prepared to recommend $15,000. Mr. Paradis, however, is asking- for $80,000 or $90,000. He has been to see me very often, and I would like to see his claim settled, although he is not legally entitled to any such amount as he asks. The last I heard of it, Mr. Paradis was asking for $30,000 or $35,000, with interest for a certain period, which would bring the claim up to $40,000. The hon. gentleman will therefore see there is quite a difference of opinion between us. I will have to get the authority of Council before I can settle the matter, but the difference between the amount asked for by the claimant and that deemed proper by the department is a little too much.
I sympathize with the old gentleman, but I am afraid I could hardly settle with him on what he is willing to accept, although he claims that if he did settle for that it

would not be one-third of what he lost. I promised the old gentleman to bring it up before a subcommittee of the Privy Council to see if we can come to terms.
During the present session?

I have been promising to do it, as a matter of fact, for the last couple of months, but it has been very hard to get members of the Council together. It is really my fault, and I will try to see if I cannot get it attended to before the end of the session.
Will the hon. member appoint me to the committee? As a member of the Privy Council I might be helpful.

I am afraid the hon. member might be partial.

Construction and Betterments, $11,121,681.

What about the Hudson Bay railway item?
Then there is item, No. 108, miscellaneous, which I think will require some explanation. It is now eleven o'clock and such an awfully hot night that I think we might better leave them over.

I would like to ask the minister regarding a matter which is very dear to the hearts of the people of Prince Edward Island; that is, the progress that the Government hope to make in the near future in broadening the gauge of the Prince Edward Island railway. Could the hon. minister gfve me some information as to the earliest possible date on which the work will be completed, as to the portion of the work he hopes to do this year, and next year, and so on; what sections of the road will be taken up in turn; and, in general, what the ideas and hopes of the Government are regarding the early completion of this work, which is so important to the people of the province from which I come.

Last year we decided to standardize the line between Port Borden and Summerside, so that cars could be loaded between those points and be brought over the main line. That work was started and proceeded with as rapidly as possible

last year. My information is that if we can get the labour next month we will be operating into .Summerside and Charlottetown with standard cars. We do not intend standardizing the line any further than Charlottetown or Summerside during the present year. After the rails are laid there will be a lot of work to do in putting the road in shape, and we feel that under present financial conditions we would not be justified in proceeding further during the present year.
It is understood, I suppose, that next year the work will be proceeded with?

It is the intention, of course, that this road should be standardized all through. I could not say how much will be done next year. But the matter will be taken up and considered with the Estimates of next year with a view of proceeding with the work when financial conditions permit.
Are details available as to how this large amount of money is going to be expended on the Canadian National railways, both with regard to construction and betterments and equipment?

I think we might as well let this item stand. I know some members of the House would like to say something on the items to which I have referred, and as the minister has made very good progress to-night, perhaps we might defer further consideration of these items.

Before the request of the leader of the Opposition is granted I wish to bring a matter to the minister's attention. I have a communication from the municipality signed by the reeve, Mr. A. A. McGillivray, and sent to me by Mr. J. McK. Hunt, with regard to changing the

name of a small station on the Canadian National railway, and I would like to have an assurance from the minister that he will try once again to get this done, as the directors do not think it convenient to take any action. As a matter of fact, the village of Slate River is some miles from the station of that name, whereas the village of Rosslyn is right there.

I did take that up with the management, and my recollection is that they claim there is another station of a similar name. However, I will take the matter up with them again.
